server_info.description: Reports on instances — the servers that are installed. With no instance_name it covers every instance at once; with one it covers that instance. The 'aspect' parameter picks what is reported. The default aspect, status, gives whether the instance is running plus its headline details, including the port it is configured to use. This covers an installed instance; blueprint_info covers a game type that is not installed.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: One instance to report on. Omitted, the report covers every instance at once, which answers a question about the whole fleet in a single call.

params.name: aspect
params.description: What to report. status (the default): whether the instance is running, and its headline details including the port it is configured to use. config: a summary of its KGSM settings, where read_file shows the raw configuration file. version: the version this instance has installed and whether an update is available — this is the instance's own installed version, where search covers what the game's developers have published. players: who is connected right now. backups: the backups it has. note: its operator note. autostart: whether it starts at boot.

host_info.description: Reports on the host machine the instances run on, rather than on any one instance.

params.name: aspect
params.description: What to report. vitals (the default): uptime, load, memory, disk, external IP, and whether a reboot is pending. ports: what is currently bound on the host. conflicts: instances configured to want the same port.

blueprint_info.description: Reports on blueprints — the game types that can be installed. With no blueprint_name it lists every blueprint. With one it describes that game type: the ports it needs, its resource requirements, and what it supports. A blueprint is a recipe, so this reports what a game type would need, never the state of anything running; server_info reports on an instance that is installed.

params.name: blueprint_name
params.description: One blueprint to describe in detail — the ports it needs, its resource needs, and what it supports — by the name it is listed under. Omitted, it lists every game type that can be installed.

events.description: The history of what has happened, read from KGSM's own event log, most recent first. Covers one instance with instance_name, or every instance without one. This is the record of what happened to this host's own instances — when one was updated, restarted, backed up or crashed. read_console gives what a server itself printed, which is a separate record.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: One instance to scope the events to. Omitted, the feed covers every instance on this host, which answers a question about the fleet in a single call.

params.name: scope
params.description: Which events to include. all (the default): the full feed — starts, stops, restarts, crashes, installs, updates, backups, port changes, player activity. changes: durable changes only — installs, uninstalls, updates, version changes, backups, port changes — which is where an instance's own update history lives, so it answers when an instance was last updated or what has changed on it. A start, a stop or a crash appears under all and not under changes.

params.name: window
params.description: How far back to look. Defaults to 24h.

run_health_check.description: A health check on one instance, returned as a ranked summary. It combines four readings in a single call: whether the instance is running, errors in its recent logs, whether an update is available, and host disk space. It describes the present; trace_root_cause investigates an incident in the past.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

get_performance.description: One instance's resource usage: CPU as a percentage of one core, memory, network and disk-I/O throughput, and process count. With no range it is a live snapshot of current values. With a range it is the trend across that window. A running instance has both. A stopped instance has no live snapshot, and may still have recent history. This covers one instance; host_info covers the machine they all run on.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: range
params.description: Optional. OMIT for a live snapshot of current usage. Provide a time window to get the TREND over that period instead (a chart of how CPU/memory changed) — use this for "how has X been doing over the last hour/day?", "is X's memory climbing?", "CPU trend for X".

get_network.description: The network reachability of one instance, across two layers: the host firewall (which ports KGSM has opened, which firewall backend, and whether it is enforcing) and the UPnP port forwards on the local router. It reports whether the instance's port is reachable; server_info reports which port the instance uses. Each layer is reported separately, and a layer that could not be reached is reported as 'couldn't check'.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

trace_root_cause.description: Investigates why one instance crashed, will not stay up, or has been misbehaving. It gathers the instance's event history, resource usage and health checks in a single call and matches them against known failure patterns — port conflicts, update-triggered crash loops, disk-full failures, mismatches between the event log and live state — then returns a ranked explanation with the evidence behind it. It covers an incident in the past; run_health_check covers the present. When no known pattern matches, it reports the correlation it found.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: range
params.description: Optional. How far back to look for evidence. Defaults to 24h if omitted.

search.description: Looks a topic up and returns short passages, each with its source — a doc path or a URL. It reads the operator's indexed documentation and the public web. It covers facts about a game or a piece of software that hold anywhere: what its settings do, what its release notes say, which version its developers have published. Facts about this host's own instances are measured directly by the KGSM tools instead — which version an instance has installed and whether an update is available come from server_info with aspect=version, and when an instance was last updated, restarted or backed up comes from events. A passage can be out of date, so it is worth citing its source and saying so.

params.name: query
params.description: The topic to look up. It covers facts about a game or a piece of software that hold anywhere — what a config option means, what a release note says, which version the developers have published. Facts about this host's own instances (status, config, health, which version is installed, when it was last updated) are measured directly by server_info and events instead.

params.name: scope
params.description: Where to look. web: the public web only, which is the source for anything that changes over time — a current version, a release date, recent news — and for anything the user asks you to check online. local: the operator's own documentation only. auto (the default): the documentation first, then the web when nothing there scores well enough. A local guide about a game matches a question about that game whether or not it addresses what was asked, so an auto result can be about the right game and silent on the question; the same words with scope=web ask a different source.

fetch_url.description: Reads the full text of one web page by its exact URL — an official docs page, a Steam store page, a raw GitHub file. It takes a URL you already have, from the user or from a search result. search is what finds a page by topic and returns short summaries; this reads one page you can already name. Public http/https pages only, and a large page is truncated.

params.name: url
params.description: The exact web address to read, including scheme — e.g. an official server-setup doc, a Steam store page, or a raw Dockerfile URL. Only public http/https pages can be fetched.

read_file.description: Reads a text file inside one instance's own directory — the game's configuration, its logs, server.properties, a mod's settings. Read-only, and confined to that instance's folder. The path is relative to the instance's directory; omitting it reads the instance's KGSM configuration (its .config.ini). Large files are truncated and binary files are not shown. A change to a game's own config file is proposed with write_file; a change to the .config.ini is proposed with set_config_value.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: path
params.description: The file to read, as a path relative to the instance's own directory — server.properties, logs/latest.log. Omitted, it reads the instance's KGSM configuration (its .config.ini). find_files locates a file by name and search_files locates one by its contents.

list_files.description: Lists the files and folders inside one instance's own directory, one level at a time. It answers what is in a directory. find_files searches every subdirectory for a file by name, and search_files searches inside every file for text.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: subdir
params.description: Optional. A subdirectory to list, relative to the server's own directory — e.g. "logs" or "install". OMIT it to list the server's top level.

find_files.description: Finds a file anywhere inside one instance's folder by name, searching every subdirectory in a single call. A game's own config often sits several directories deep, so one glob reaches it where stepping down a level at a time takes many calls. It returns matching paths ready to pass to read_file. Archived copies under a backups folder are excluded, so what comes back is the live file.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: pattern
params.description: The file name as a glob — PalWorldSettings.ini, *.ini, server.properties, *Settings*. A / in the pattern matches against the path rather than the name, e.g. */Config/*.ini. The most specific pattern that fits returns the fewest files; a broad one can match hundreds.

params.name: subdir
params.description: Optional. Search only inside this subdirectory of the server's folder. OMIT it to search the whole server directory, which is usually what you want.

search_files.description: Searches inside one instance's files for text, across every subdirectory in a single call. It finds which file holds a setting when the setting's name is known and the file's is not — MaxPlayers, DayTimeSpeedRate. It returns each matching file with the line number and the line itself, ready to pass to read_file. find_files searches by file name instead. Archived copies under a backups folder are excluded, and binary files are skipped.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: text
params.description: The text to look for inside the files — a setting name such as MaxPlayers or DayTimeSpeedRate. Matching ignores case and a regular expression works. This is file content rather than a file name, so it takes the bare text with no * around it. A distinctive string returns the fewest lines; a common word can match hundreds.

params.name: subdir
params.description: Optional. Search only inside this subdirectory of the server's folder. OMIT it to search the whole server directory, which is usually what you want.

read_console.description: Reads what an instance itself printed — its console output. It covers what an instance is saying now, and what it said on its way down; a stopped instance's last output is still readable. events covers KGSM's own record of what happened to the instance, which is a separate record from what the game printed. The reply names which run it came from and whether the instance restarted recently. An instance's log restarts from empty every time it starts, so after a crash-restart the crash is in run 1 and run 0 holds the clean boot that followed it.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: lines
params.description: Optional. How many of the most recent console lines to read. Defaults to a recent tail.

params.name: run
params.description: Optional. Which run of the server to read, newest first: 0 is the current run (the default), 1 the run before it, and so on. A server's log restarts from empty every time it starts, so after a crash-restart the crash is in run 1 while run 0 holds only the clean boot that followed it.

server_command.description: Proposes a lifecycle action on one existing instance, chosen with the 'verb' parameter. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: verb
params.description: Which action to take. start: run a stopped instance now. stop: stop a running one. restart: stop it and start it again. update: bring it to its latest version. backup: take one now. enable_autostart and disable_autostart: whether it starts when the host boots. start acts now, and enable_autostart acts at the next boot.

backup_command.description: Proposes acting on an instance's existing backups: restore one over the instance's current data, delete one, or prune the old ones. server_info with aspect=backups lists them under the id this tool takes. Restoring replaces the instance's current data, and deleting is permanent. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: verb
params.description: What to do with the instance's existing backups. restore: replace the instance's current data with a backup. delete: remove one backup. prune: delete the oldest, keeping the most recent few. server_command with verb=backup creates a new one.

params.name: backup_name
params.description: Which backup to act on, by its id from server_info(aspect=backups). Required for restore and delete; omit it for prune.

params.name: keep
params.description: For prune only: how many of the most recent backups to keep. Omit for the server's configured retention.

player_command.description: Proposes moderating a player on one instance: kick, ban, or unban them. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms. Moderation works on games whose server supports moderation commands, and the tool reports when a game does not.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: verb
params.description: What to do with the player: kick (disconnect them now), ban (disconnect and block them), or unban (lift a ban).

params.name: target
params.description: Which player, exactly as the user named them. server_info with aspect=players lists who is connected. The game decides which form of identifier it needs and the system supplies it, so the name as the user gave it is the right thing to pass.

install_server.description: Proposes installing a new instance from a blueprint. The blueprint is the game type; the instance is the server this creates from it. Heavy and slow. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms.

params.name: blueprint_name
params.description: The blueprint to install, by the name it is listed under, e.g. "Project Zomboid".

params.name: instance_name
params.description: Optional custom name for the new instance. Omit to let the system name it.

params.name: version
params.description: Optional. A specific version to install. Omit for the latest, which is almost always right.

params.name: port
params.description: Optional. Override the blueprint's primary game port. Omit unless the user asked for a specific port or a conflict needs avoiding.

uninstall_server.description: Proposes permanently deleting one instance and all of its data. Irreversible. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

set_config_value.description: Proposes setting one key=value in an instance's KGSM configuration (its .config.ini) — settings such as auto_update, executable_arguments, or a timeout. A change to the game's own config file is proposed with set_game_setting (one Key=Value setting) or write_file (any other edit) instead. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms. kgsm keeps identity and structural keys, path keys (*_dir and *_file), ports, and the integration toggles (enable_firewall_management, enable_port_forwarding, enable_command_shortcuts) to their own dedicated flows, so one of those is rejected at confirmation time and the tool says which.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: config_key
params.description: The configuration key to set, e.g. "auto_update", "executable_arguments", or "stop_command_timeout_seconds".

params.name: config_value
params.description: The new value for the key. Pass an empty string to clear the setting.

write_file.description: Proposes a change to a text file inside one instance's own directory — the game's own config file, such as Palworld's PalWorldSettings.ini, server.properties, or a mod's settings file. It takes only the text that changes: old_string is the exact text to replace, copied from read_file's output, and new_string is what it becomes. The rest of the file is preserved byte for byte. old_string has to match exactly once; a match in no place, or in several, stages nothing and returns an error saying which, and reading the file again for the exact text resolves it. set_game_setting changes one Key=Value setting by naming its key, which needs no copied text and is the way to change a setting in a config that packs every setting onto one line; KGSM's own settings (ports, launch arguments, auto-update) are proposed with set_config_value. Staged for human confirmation against a preview: it does not run until a person confirms, and a running instance picks the change up on its next restart.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: path
params.description: The file to change, as a path relative to the instance's own directory — install/Pal/Saved/Config/LinuxServer/PalWorldSettings.ini, server.properties. find_files locates it by name and read_file shows its contents.

params.name: old_string
params.description: The exact text to replace, copied character for character from what read_file showed you — normally the one setting being changed, e.g. "Difficulty=None". It has to appear exactly once in the file; where it appears more than once, a little of the surrounding text narrows it to one place. Everything else in the file is preserved for you.

params.name: new_string
params.description: What that text becomes, e.g. "Difficulty=Difficulty_Hard". To add a setting, put a nearby existing line in old_string and that same line plus the new one here. An empty value deletes the old text.

params.name: copy_from
params.description: For a file that is empty or does not exist yet, when the game ships a default or reference file beside it (e.g. "install/DefaultPalWorldSettings.ini"): its content is copied into the file server-side and the old_string/new_string replacement is applied to that copy. Left out when editing a file that already has content.

create_blueprint.description: Authors a blueprint for a game that is missing from the catalog. It runs its own online research and drafts a server config in a single call, then shows the draft to the user in an editor to review and tweak. Calling it is what starts the research and the drafting, so it is the whole first step and needs no search, fetch_url or blueprint_info call ahead of it. The test-install and verification run later, when the user saves the config, so that is the point at which the game is added. blueprint_info lists the games already in the catalog, and a game already there is installed with install_server. Not every game can be self-hosted or has a native Linux server, and the tool reports either outcome.

params.name: game
params.description: The game to add, by its common name — "Terraria", "Rust". A blueprint slug is not what this takes.

revise_blueprint.description: Updates the blueprint draft the user is currently reviewing in the editor — a metadata field (min or recommended RAM, max players, disk), a port, the launch args, any part of it. The draft's current YAML is given in this turn's context; revised_yaml takes that whole document with the requested change applied. It re-validates and shows the updated draft to review and save, and installs nothing. This tool is what changes an open draft, and the change is real once it returns successfully.

params.name: revised_yaml
params.description: The complete updated blueprint YAML: the whole document, being the open draft's current content with the requested change applied. It is the full document rather than a fragment or a diff, and every field the user did not ask about keeps its current value.

set_game_setting.description: Proposes changing one Key=Value setting in a game's own config file, naming the setting by its key. The value currently on disk is read here, so only the key and the new value are sent and the rest of the file is preserved byte for byte. This works whichever shape the config has — one setting per line, or every setting packed onto a single line, which is where naming the surrounding text stops being possible. The reply names the value that was there before. write_file covers a change that is not one setting's value, such as adding a line or editing prose; set_config_value covers KGSM's own settings rather than the game's. Staged for human confirmation: it does not run until a person confirms, and a running instance picks the change up on its next restart.

params.name: instance_name
params.description: The exact name of the server instance.

params.name: path
params.description: The game's own config file. Its NAME is enough — "PalWorldSettings.ini", "server.properties" — and it is looked up under the instance, so the directories around it do not have to be right. A full path works too. When the name matches several files, the reply lists them and a full path picks one; search_files finds the file that carries a given setting.

params.name: setting
params.description: The setting's key on its own, without an '=' or the rest of the line — "DayTimeSpeedRate", "Difficulty", "max-players". Case does not have to match the file. The key has to be set exactly once in the file; a key set in two places is reported rather than guessed at.

params.name: value
params.description: The value the setting becomes, written exactly as the file spells values — "0.500000", "Difficulty_Hard", "20". Quotes are part of the value where the file quotes it. An empty string clears the value and keeps the setting.

params.name: copy_from
params.description: For a config that is empty or does not exist yet, when the game ships a default or reference file beside it (e.g. "install/DefaultPalWorldSettings.ini"): its content is copied in server-side and the setting changed on that copy. Left out when editing a file that already has content.
